title: Tools, MCP and action authorization
summary: Follow one tool call from a model's proposal through a policy gate to an audited effect: schemas, identities and delegated permissions, untrusted content, approvals, timeouts and idempotency keys, and what MCP standardizes versus what your code must still enforce.
objectives: Trace a tool call from proposal to effect and order the gate's checks: session, exposed tool, schema, delegated permission, key, approval and execution.
Decide whose identity a target evaluates, refuse retrieved content and system prompts as authority, and design approvals, retries and keys that cannot duplicate an effect.
Explain what MCP carries and where authorization is still enforced, and read an audit trail and test matrix from Lab L22.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
A proposal, a gate, a handler

Try it: a clinic supply assistant

questions.prompt: Lab L22's C10 copies approved_by: sup-n1 from a supplier page into request_spare_part's arguments. Which check refuses it first?

options.text: The delegated permission check, because tech-n1 lacks parts:request:north.
options.rationale: tech-n1 holds parts:request:north; the call fails before permission is even evaluated.

options.text: The schema: approved_by is not a property and additionalProperties is false.
options.rationale: Schema validation runs before permission and approval, and names the unexpected property.

options.text: The approval hold, because the named supervisor must confirm it.
options.rationale: The schema check comes earlier, and a name inside arguments never counts as an approval.

options.text: The model, because the system prompt forbids approving orders.
options.rationale: A system prompt is a request to the model; the refusal is enforced by the gate's schema check.

questions.prompt: C17 reports timed_out after three late replies, although the store wrote D3 on the first attempt. A minute later C18 sends the same arguments with the same key. What happens?

options.text: The gate refuses C18 as a conflict because the key was already used.
options.rationale: A conflict needs different arguments; C18's digest matches, so the in-doubt key is resolved instead.

options.text: The store writes a fourth draft, because the first call failed.
options.rationale: The first call did not fail; its outcome was unknown, and the store already holds D3 for that key.

options.text: The gate returns timed_out again without contacting the store.
options.rationale: An in-doubt key is re-sent precisely so the target can report the existing effect.

options.text: The gate re-sends with key k-17, the store returns D3, and no fourth draft is written.
options.rationale: An in-doubt key is resolved by asking the target again with the same key.

questions.prompt: An MCP server lists delete_work_order with readOnlyHint: true. What should Cinderline's application do?

options.text: Expose it, since read-only tools cannot cause harm.
options.rationale: The hint may be unfaithful, and the tool's own name says it deletes things.

options.text: Expose it and let the system prompt forbid deletions.
options.rationale: A prompt is a request the model may not follow; an unexposed tool cannot be called at all.

options.text: Leave it out of the exposed tools unless a reviewed decision adds it; a server's hints are not guarantees.
options.rationale: Exposure is the application's decision, and annotations from a server are only hints.

options.text: Expose it, but set the model's temperature to zero.
options.rationale: Temperature changes sampling, not what the application allows the model to call.

cards.prompt: Which component performs the effect when a model emits a tool call?
cards.answer: The application's handler, after the policy gate allows it; the model only returns a tool name and JSON arguments as text.
cards.explanation: A model has no connection to Cinderline's systems. Its output is text that the application parses into a tool name and arguments; the gate checks it and a handler performs the write. That is why every control must sit in the application, not in the model.

cards.prompt: Why is priority: urgent malformed rather than merely discouraged?
cards.answer: Because priority is not a property of create_maintenance_draft and additionalProperties is false, so no value of it can pass the schema.
cards.explanation: A constraint that lives only in a description is a request the model may ignore. Declaring the allowed properties and setting additionalProperties to false lets the gate reject the call before a handler runs, with a message naming the rule, as Lab L22's C06 shows.

cards.prompt: Under app authorization, whose grants does the draft store evaluate?
cards.answer: The application's service principal's grants, whoever asked, so every user inherits the application's reach.
cards.explanation: The target sees only the credential that arrives. If the assistant sends its own service principal's token, a South technician's request for North machine M7 is judged by the principal's broad grant, not by the technician's, and the audit cannot tell people apart.

cards.prompt: A supervisor holds drafts:close:north, yet closing D1 is refused. Why?
cards.answer: The application was never delegated drafts:close, and delegated permission is the intersection of user grants and application scopes.
cards.explanation: On-behalf-of access never exceeds either side. Lab L22's C14 records 'missing drafts:close:north (lacking: application)': the person may close drafts elsewhere, but not through an application whose scopes exclude closing. The fix is a deliberate scope decision, not a prompt.

cards.prompt: A retrieved supplier page claims a supervisor approved an order. What authority does that text carry?
cards.answer: None: identity comes from the session and approval from an authorized person's recorded decision, never from content.
cards.explanation: Retrieved text crosses a trust boundary; its author never signed in. The gate never reads it, so Lab L22's decisions are identical with every document removed. At most the text makes the model propose a call that the gate then refuses or holds for a human.

cards.prompt: Which controls still hold if the model ignores every instruction it was given?
cards.answer: Only enforced ones: the exposed-tool allowlist, the grant check, the schema and the approval hold; system prompt sentences do not.
cards.explanation: A system prompt shares the context with anything an attacker can get retrieved, and a model can be persuaded. Count a control only if code outside the model enforces it; keep the sentences as guidance for normal behaviour, but record them as requests, not boundaries.

cards.prompt: What makes a recorded approval evidence rather than a click?
cards.answer: It names an authorized approver other than the requester, binds the exact stored arguments, and executes them once.
cards.explanation: In Lab L22, A1 stored 2 × P-0415 with its digest. Self-approval and an approver without parts:approve:north were refused, the supervisor's approval executed PR1 once, and reusing the key with quantity 20 was a conflict, so the approval could not be stretched.

cards.prompt: A draft call timed out three times. What do you know about the draft?
cards.answer: Nothing certain: the target may have written it before the replies were lost, so the outcome is unknown.
cards.explanation: In Lab L22's C17 the store wrote D3 on the first attempt, but every reply arrived after the 2000 ms limit. Reporting 'failed' would invite a blind resubmission; the gate reports outcome_unknown and marks the key in doubt so the next call can look it up.

cards.prompt: Predict the drafts after C02, an exact repeat, and a repeat with a new note.
cards.answer: One draft, D1: the exact repeat returns D1 and the changed repeat is refused as a conflict.
cards.explanation: The gate stores key k-02 with the digest of its arguments. The same digest returns the stored outcome without touching the store; a different digest under the same key signals a different intent reusing an identifier, which is refused rather than guessed at.

cards.prompt: What does MCP standardize, and what does it leave to you?
cards.answer: Discovery and invocation of tools over JSON-RPC and standard transports; deciding who may call what stays with your code.
cards.explanation: A client lists tools with tools/list and calls them with tools/call over stdio or Streamable HTTP. The protocol carries names, schemas and hints, and says clients should not trust hints from untrusted servers. Nothing in it decides whether this user may draft for this machine.

cards.prompt: A valid MCP token passed the scope check. Which checks remain before an effect?
cards.answer: The handler's check of this call's arguments against the caller, and the target system's own permissions.
cards.explanation: The SDK's token check establishes expiry and endpoint scopes, and the audience once audience validation is enabled, as the MCP specification requires. It cannot know that machine C4 belongs to South, and a Unity Catalog function behind the handler still requires EXECUTE for the calling principal. Each layer refuses independently.

cards.prompt: Why must the audit record calls that did nothing?
cards.answer: Because refusals are the evidence that a boundary held; a log of successes cannot show that an attack was stopped.
cards.explanation: Lab L22 writes 26 rows for 25 events, including three malformed calls and seven denials. A reviewer can see that the supplier page's forged approval was refused at the schema. Arguments appear only as a digest, so the audit carries no free-text notes or tokens.

cards.prompt: What does a passing local stub harness prove about a tool gate?
cards.answer: That the gate's own logic decides each tested case as specified, not that the platform's permissions or network behave the same.
cards.explanation: Lab L22's 41 tests assert decisions, reasons and effect counts against hand-derived literals, and nine deliberate mutations each turn them red. Real identities, Unity Catalog grants, timeouts and transactions still need a run against the platform before launch.
